## What you just did, as a flowchart and a checklist
:::

```{=html}
<div id="b2-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Time stamps</dt><dd>EIA-930 stamps each hour in <span class="lx-term" data-term="utc">UTC</span> at its end; label hours by their start and convert to local time before grouping by day.</dd>
<dt>Range, repeats, physics</dt><dd>Three checks flag three kinds of suspect data: a spike, a possibly stuck feed, and sun at night.</dd>
<dt>Mean or sum</dt><dd>Average power uses the mean; energy uses the sum, since each hour's MW × 1 h is its MWh.</dd>
<dt><span class="lx-term" data-term="duration-curve">Duration curve</span></dt><dd>The year's hours sorted from highest to lowest; for a plant, the area under it over the full box is the capacity factor.</dd>
<dt>Assert</dt><dd>A check that stops the notebook with a message when the data break a rule.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Why one hour of offset matters to a model</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>An hourly model reads value <em>t</em> as the average power over hour <em>t</em>, the hour its time stamp labels; times one hour, that is its energy.</li>
<li>Shift the stamps by one hour and the solar peak moves an hour, which changes when a battery should charge and what it earns.</li>
<li>Days of 23 and 25 hours break code that assumes 24 rows a day: keep a time-zone-aware index and let pandas place each hour.</li>
</ul>
<p>Modeler's note: the lab's notebook is the template for every later lab; <a href="m10-ml-forecasting.html">M10</a> (forecasting) and, upcoming, M14 (learning from data) start from a frame checked like this one.</p>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>A capacity factor needs a capacity</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>A capacity factor is energy divided by (nameplate capacity × hours). EIA-930 reports generation, not capacity, so a real fleet's capacity factor needs a second source, such as EIA's generator inventory (Form EIA-860).</p>
<p>Observed peak output is not a capacity measurement. If it is below nameplate capacity, using it as the denominator overstates the capacity factor.</p>
<p>Prairie Town's farms are defined to reach full output in SPP's best hour, which is why their 52.8% and 23.4% are labelled illustrative. <a href="05-capacity-factor.html">Lesson 5</a> builds capacity factors from scratch.</p>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>How the data build filled the gaps, and its night rule</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<table class="lx-facts">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Problem</th><th scope="col">What the data build did</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Repeated wind or solar readings</td><td>Replaced by the mean of the same hour on up to seven valid days before and after.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Implausible demand hours</td><td>Replaced by the day-ahead forecast, rescaled to the actual demand around the gap.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Solar at night, 20 February to 14 March</td><td>Raw solar barely changed between day and night but never repeated exactly, so the repeat rule kept it. A night rule sets solar to zero.</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<ul>
<li><b>The night rule</b> is a documented heuristic for this SPP, Central-time example: hours whose monthly median solar is zero, 22:00 to 05:00 all year, and hours when the sun is below the horizon at SPP's centre.</li>
<li><b>What it proves.</b> Hours set to zero pass a night check by construction; the check does not test the daytime values, so look at those too.</li>
<li>The notebook applies the median and clock parts of the rule to the raw file.</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="r04-data.html">R4</a> (data you can defend) turns these choices into a written data note.</p>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

::: {#check .lx-sec}

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="b2-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="day" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Every local day has 24 hours.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Where clocks change for <span class="lx-term" data-term="daylight-saving-time">daylight saving</span>, one spring day has 23 hours and one autumn day has 25; in 2025 in U.S. Central time, 9 March and 2 November.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="summary" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If the summary statistics look normal, every row is fine.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. 617 MW is a normal solar value, but not at 2 a.m.; repeat and physics checks look at rows and their times, not just at summaries.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cf" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Average wind output divided by the year's best hour is the wind fleet's capacity factor.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A <span class="lx-term" data-term="capacity-factor">capacity factor</span> divides by nameplate capacity. The best hour is not a capacity measurement; if it is below nameplate, that ratio overstates the capacity factor.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="b2">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="mwh" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A wind farm's hourly output is 100 MW in every hour of one 24-hour day. How much <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy">energy</span> did it make that day?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">100 MWh</li><li data-value="b">2,400 MWh</li><li data-value="c">4.2 MW</li><li data-value="d">2,400 MW</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>2,400 MWh: energy = power × time, 100 MW × 24 h. On a 23- or 25-hour day it would be 2,300 or 2,500 MWh.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="sum" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">You resample hourly MW values to months. Which gives each month's energy?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">The mean</li><li data-value="b">The sum</li><li data-value="c">The maximum</li><li data-value="d">The median</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>The sum, in MWh (divide by 1,000 for GWh). The mean gives the month's average power in MW.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::
